titre: Johnson, 1755: The Dictionary That Said It Couldn't Fix English
accroche: They say Johnson's Dictionary fixed English. His 1755 preface says a dictionary can't do that, and that its author believed it could, for a while.
contenu_vulgarise:
Samuel Johnson's *Dictionary of the English Language*, published in London in 1755, is often presented as the book that fixed English: an arbiter of spelling, Britain's answer to an academy. Open its preface and you read almost the opposite, in Johnson's own hand.

## A Hope, Then a Doubt

In paragraph 84 of the preface (numbering from Jack Lynch's abridged edition), Johnson reports what his readers expect of him: that the book will fix the language and halt the changes that time and chance have brought to it without opposition. He admits that he flattered himself with this idea for a while, then came to fear he had nourished an expectation that neither reason nor experience justifies. He compares the lexicographer who would imagine he could embalm his language to the elixir said to prolong life to 1,000 years, which people rightly laugh at, and notes that no nation has ever preserved its words and phrases from mutability.

## Academies, a Poor Example

The next paragraph targets the academies, set up to guard the avenues of their languages, to retain fugitives and repulse intruders. Their vigilance, he writes, has been vain. French has visibly changed under the inspection of the Academy, and no Italian would maintain that the prose of a modern author does not differ from that of Boccaccio, Machiavelli, or Caro. The line that endures from this passage, quoted in this entry, ranks the project of controlling syllables among the undertakings of pride.

## Neither Clerk Nor Lawgiver

Johnson is not, for all that, a mere clerk. He judges the spelling of his time to be unstable and left to chance. He distinguishes the irregularities native to English, which must be recorded, from those produced by the ignorance or negligence of later writers. Every language also has, he adds, its improprieties and absurdities, which it is the lexicographer's duty to correct or proscribe. But when he decides, it is often in favor of usage: in paragraph 13, he writes *convey* and *inveigh*, *deceit* and *receipt*, out of deference to an innumerable majority, even at the cost of sacrificing uniformity to custom. In paragraph 69, he concedes that the spelling he recommends remains open to dispute.

The position he gives himself comes down to a few words in paragraph 91: if the changes one fears are irresistible, what remains is to delay what cannot be repelled and to ease what cannot be cured.

## What This Shifts

The dictionary did indeed weigh on usage, because it backed its 42,773 words with some 114,000 quotations drawn from about 500 authors (figures from the Wikipedia entry). This influence comes from the work, not from a doctrine: in his preface, its author gives up any claim to lock English down. The legend of Johnson as lawgiver confuses what the book produced with what its preface promised.

One question remains that the preface leaves open: does what is attributed to this dictionary belong to its author, or to those who chose it as their reference?

carte.punch: Johnson, 1755: fixing a language with a dictionary is like lashing the wind.
carte.idee: They say Johnson's dictionary fixed English. In his 1755 preface, he admits he cherished that hope for a while, then compares the lexicographer who would embalm his language to the elixir of long life that people laugh at. He promises only to delay what he cannot repel.

quiz.question: What does Johnson say in his 1755 preface about the hope that his dictionary would fix the language?
choix: That the book succeeded, as the French Academy did for the French language
That an academy would succeed better than a lexicographer working almost alone
That he hoped for it for a while, then judged the expectation unjustified by reason and experience alike
That the project is absurd, since English has no spelling yet to fix
quiz.explication: In paragraph 84, Johnson admits he flattered himself with this hope for a while, then feared an expectation that neither reason nor experience justifies. In the next paragraph, he judges the vigilance of the academies vain: French has visibly changed under the inspection of its own. He doesn't give up acting, though, since he proposes to delay what cannot be repelled, and he recognizes the spelling of his day as unstable, not absent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Johnson reproach the academies charged with guarding a language, in the paragraph after his quoted line?
choix: They succeeded in fixing spelling for good, unlike a lone lexicographer
They existed in no European country before the publication of his dictionary
They merely copied existing English dictionaries
Their vigilance was in vain: French has visibly changed under the Academy's inspection
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Johnson judges the academies' vigilance vain: he notes that French has visibly changed under the Academy's inspection, despite its mission to retain fugitives.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Johnson choose, in paragraph 13 of his preface, for words like convey and inveigh?
choix: He imposes a single new spelling for each pair of homophones
He keeps the existing spellings out of deference to usage, even at the cost of uniformity
He leaves the decision to an academy he proposes founding after his dictionary
He drops one of the two words in each pair as superfluous
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Johnson writes convey and inveigh, deceit and receipt out of deference to an innumerable majority, even at the cost of sacrificing uniformity of spelling to established custom.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 1755 Dictionary rest on to weigh on English usage, according to the Wikipedia entry cited in the write-up?
choix: A committee of 50 lexicographers assembled on the model of the French Academy
Only quotations drawn from Shakespeare's plays and the King James Bible
About 114,000 quotations drawn from about 500 authors, for 42,773 words
A list of about 5,000 words approved by the royal court of England
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Wikipedia entry gives 42,773 words backed by some 114,000 quotations drawn from about 500 authors: it is this mass of quotations that weighed on usage.
